title: Did Community Rating Induce an Adverse Selection Death Spiral?
research_question: Did the imposition of pure community rating on small group and individual health insurance markets cause an adverse selection death spiral, in which younger and healthier consumers drop coverage, the insured pool ages, and overall insurance coverage declines? Relatedly, did such rating restrictions alter the composition of insurance products purchased, for example by shifting enrollment between indemnity coverage and HMOs?
data_description: The primary data come from the March Current Population Surveys for 1988–1997, with insurance questions referring to coverage in the prior calendar year, yielding a sample period of 1987–1996. The unit of observation is a civilian adult aged 18–64 in New York, Pennsylvania, or Connecticut. Key variables include indicators for any private health insurance, employer-sponsored coverage, private coverage in own name, and uninsured status, along with demographics (age, sex, race, ethnicity, education, marital status, student status, location), employment characteristics (full/part-time, class of worker, industry, firm size split at 100 employees), and self-employment. Supplementary data include employer surveys from the Health Insurance Association of America (1988–1991) and KPMG/Peat Marwick (1993, 1995) on HMO offerings, plus New York State Department of Insurance demographic risk factors for Blue Cross/Blue Shield, commercial indemnity insurers, and HMOs from 1993–1996.
institutional_context: During the early 1990s, 45 U.S. states regulated their small group health insurance markets to limit insurer practices that disadvantaged high-risk small firms. New York enacted the most far-reaching reforms, effective April 1993, imposing pure community rating—identical premiums regardless of age, sex, or risk—along with guaranteed issue, guaranteed renewal, and limits on preexisting condition exclusions in both the small group and individual markets. Connecticut, effective June 1991, adopted more moderate reforms applying only to small groups, permitting adjusted community rating that allowed premiums to vary by age, gender, region, industry, group size, and coverage tier. Pennsylvania enacted no such reforms. The three states are geographically proximate, demographically similar, and faced comparable business-cycle conditions, with closely correlated unemployment rates, providing a natural setting to assess how community rating affects coverage and plan choice.
